title: PSK2a is required for cambial development and xylem formation during secondary growth in poplar.
authors: Yue, Songqing; Tian, Dongdong; Ma, Xiao; Qi, Cheng; Wan, Mengjie; Qi, Juan; Cheng, Qian; Tian, Lidan; Shi, Xueping; Zheng, Bo
abstract: Phytosulfokines (PSKs) are sulfated peptide hormones involved in plant growth, development, and stress responses. However, direct genetic evidence for the involvement of PSK peptide in cambium development and secondary vascular development in woody plants remains largely lacking. Here, we identified nine PSK family members in Populus trichocarpa. Phylogenetic, gene structure, conserved motif, and local synteny analyses indicated that the poplar PSK family is evolutionarily conserved, and some members may have arisen from the whole-genome duplication (WGD) event. PSK2a is one of several PSK family genes that are highly expressed in poplar stem vascular tissues, but shows low expression in roots. Subsequently, we generated PtrPSK2a (cloned from P. trichocarpa) overexpression lines in hybrid poplar 717 and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout lines targeting its endogenous orthologs PtaPSK2a_HAP1 and HAP2hybrid poplar 717. Both gain-of-function and loss-of-function of PSK2a exhibited growth defects, characterized by reduced plant height and stem diameter, with more severe overall growth defects in OE lines. Consistently, histological analysis demonstrated that cambium activity and secondary xylem development were significantly inhibited in both transgenic lines, as reflected by fewer cambium cell layers, narrower xylem, and fewer vessels in young stems. In addition, genes associated with cambial development, vessel differentiation, and secondary cell wall formation were broadly downregulated, accompanied by altered expression of several hormone-related marker genes in transgenic lines. Together, these findings demonstrate that PSK2a is required for normal cambial activity and xylem development during secondary growth in poplar, providing the first direct genetic evidence for PSK function in woody plant vascular development.

title: A novel FRET-force biosensor for nucleoporin gp210 reveals that the nuclear pore complex experiences mechanical tension.
authors: Wang, Peipei; Denis, Kevin; Luxton, G W Gant; Conway, Daniel E
abstract: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is a large multi-protein structure that enables movement of macromolecules, such as mRNA and proteins, between the nucleoplasm and cytoplasm. There has been great interest in how the physical state of the NPC can influence nuclear-cytoplasmic transport. The hypothesis that the NPC may be mechanosensitive is supported by prior reports showing that the diameter of the NPC increases with nuclear envelope stretch as well as increased ECM stiffness. We therefore sought to develop a biosensor-based approach to determine if the NPC experiences mechanical tension. Using a previously developed FRET-force biosensor, known as TSMod, we developed a gp210 tension sensor. gp210 is a transmembrane nucleoporin, which may serve to anchor the NPC into the nuclear envelope. Using a CRISPR knock-in strategy, we developed a HeLa cell line which expresses the gp210 tension sensor at endogenous levels. The FRET-force responsiveness of the gp210 tension sensor was validated using hypo-osmotic and hyper-osmotic nuclear swelling experiments. Additionally, we observed that gp210 forces are sensitive to the ECM, nuclear LINC complex, chromatin condensation, and actomyosin contractility. Our results indicate that both nuclear strain and cytoskeletal forces contribute to mechanical tension across gp210. Our studies provide the first direct measurements of protein-level mechanical forces on the NPC. We anticipate that the gp210 force sensor will be of use for future studies of NPC mechanobiology.

title: A comprehensive review of mixed-species biofilm infections and innovative therapeutic strategies.
authors: Nazari, Mohsen; Kardan, Romina; Ahmadi, Amjad; Abolhasani, Fatemeh Sadat; Hemmati, Jaber
abstract: Mixed-species biofilm infections are important causes of persistent and difficult-to-treat infections. Compared with monospecies biofilms, mixed-species communities contain microorganisms with different physiological and genetic characteristics that interact through metabolic cooperation, chemical signaling, competition, and modification of the local environment. These interactions, together with the EPS matrix, physiological heterogeneity, and HGT, can increase antimicrobial tolerance, contributing to treatment failure and infection recurrence. Polymicrobial biofilms are associated with chronic wounds, respiratory infections, catheter- and device-associated infections, and other persistent infections. However, treatment of polymicrobial biofilms remains challenging because their complex structure and interspecies interactions can reduce antimicrobial efficacy. This review summarizes the clinical significance, formation, and persistence of mixed-species biofilms and discusses recent therapeutic strategies for their control. We also discuss recent approaches for controlling polymicrobial biofilms, including natural compounds, QS inhibition, CRISPR-Cas-based approaches, biofilm matrix targeting, metabolic and nutrient disruption, nanotechnology, and phage therapy. Recent studies show that these approaches can inhibit biofilm formation, disrupt established biofilms, enhance antimicrobial activity, and selectively target specific microbial populations. However, their effectiveness varies with microbial composition, biofilm maturity, matrix characteristics, and treatment conditions. Overall, current evidence supports the development of targeted and combination-based strategies for mixed-species biofilms. Further studies using clinically relevant models are needed to exactly define treatment efficacy and support the translation of these approaches into clinical practice.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-out of abnormal chemosensory jump 6 (acj6) gene impacts Helicoverpa armigera antennal lobe structure.
authors: Xie, Guiying; Chen, Shuting; Sun, Longlong; Chu, Xi; Lu, Jing; Khalid, Muhammad Lubaid; Lin, Rongmei; Chen, Wenbo; Zhao, Xincheng
abstract: The specificity of the olfactory system in the brain is determined not only by the expression of odorant receptor genes but also by the specific neural circuit assembly within the antennal lobe (AL). To investigate the developmental role of abnormal chemosensory jump 6 (acj6) in the moth Helicoverpa armigera, we generated Haacj6 mutants using CRISPR/Cas9 and examined the detailed structure of the AL based on immunostaining and three-dimensional reconstruction. The results showed that the AL in male Haacj6 mutants was markedly enlarged. In both sexes, the AL of Haacj6 mutants contained approximately 100 glomeruli, compared with about 75 glomeruli in wild-type. Glomerular volumes were also more heterogeneous in the mutants: the largest glomeruli were expanded, whereas the smallest were reduced, although the mean glomerular volume remained unchanged. These results demonstrate that the Haacj6 gene plays a critical role in normal AL development and that AL enlargement in the mutants arises primarily from the presence of additional glomeruli. These additional glomeruli likely reflect defects in olfactory receptor neuron axon wiring to AL projection neurons, or glial mediated glomerular boundary formation. These findings indicate that acj6 is an essential regulator of AL architecture and provide crucial insights into the molecular mechanisms governing neural circuits assembly in insects.

title: Structure- and Exonuclease-Guided Engineering of Cas12o1 Enhances Genome Editing Efficiency and Deletion Outcomes.
authors: Wang, Linli; Wang, Yanlu; He, Xiaoya; Chen, Jian; Ai, Yue; Han, Hongbing
abstract: Small and efficient CRISPR nucleases hold great promise for genome engineering but often exhibit suboptimal activity and limited control over DNA repair outcomes. Here, we engineer Cas12o1 using a structure- and exonuclease-guided strategy to enhance both editing efficiency and deletion profiles in mammalian cells. Structure-guided arginine-scanning mutagenesis of 42 residues identifies a single substitution, D534R, that markedly improves editing efficiency across multiple genomic loci, outperforming combinatorial variants. In parallel, fusion of T5 exonuclease (T5 exo) profoundly remodels DNA repair outcomes, strongly enriching long-fragment deletions without compromising overall activity. Integrating the D534R mutation with T5 exo fusion increases Cas12o1 editing efficiency by 1.2-1.9-fold and yields a higher proportion of deletions exceeding 10 bp. Notably, at selected loci such as HBB, the enhanced Cas12o1-T5 exonuclease (enCas12o1-T5 exo) achieved comparable or higher editing efficiencies than canonical SpCas9 and LbCas12a. Together, these results establish a rational framework for simultaneously enhancing the efficiency and repair outcomes of compact CRISPR nucleases, expanding the genome-engineering potential of Cas12o1.

title: Two novel phosphodiesterases (PDEs) found from woody plant jujube exhibit diverse biological functions via regulating cAMP, cGMP and hormones.
authors: Zhao, Xin; Wang, Di; Deng, Xiaofeng; Mai, Junyan; Liu, Zhiguo; Liu, Mengjun
abstract: Phosphodiesterases (PDEs) are the key enzymes hydrolyzing cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) and cGMP (cyclic guanosine monophosphate), two important second messengers triggering many physiological responses, and regulating growth, development and defense in plants. As the identification of PDEs from plants is really puzzling, only very few herbaceous plant PDEs have been functionally verified, and the biological functions of plant PDEs are still unclear. Here, we identified two novel PDE genes (ZjPDE1 and ZjPDE2) of cAMP/cGMP dual-specificity from a woody plant jujube (Ziziphus jujuba Mill.) known for its fruit rich in cAMP and cGMP. The two PDE genes have very poor sequence similarity but quite similar secondary structure, motif, and binding mode to cAMP/cGMP. Their phosphodiesterase activities were verified via in vitro catalytic assays, in vivo transient overexpression, and stable genetic transformation. After knocking out the homologous sequences of ZjPDE1 and ZjPDE2 in model plant tomato via CRISPR/Cas9, the mutants, compared to WT, showed increased cAMP/cGMP accumulation, accelerated seed germination, promoted flowering, as well as advanced fruiting and coloration, which were largely consist with the effects of spraying cAMP/cGMP. These biological functions are the combined effects of cAMP and cGMP cross talking with phytohorones including GA and ABA. These results demonstrate that ZjPDE1 and ZjPDE2 are functional PDEs capable of hydrolyzing cAMP and cGMP, and PDE-mediated cAMP/cGMP signaling may crosstalk with phytohormone pathways such as IAA, GA and ABA, to regulate plant growth, flowering and fruiting.

title: Reshaping the scissors: From directed evolution to AI-driven design for enhanced Cas performance.
authors: Cheng, Xinrui; Ruan, Weimin; Jin, Zheng; Suo, Langda; Ma, Yuehui; Jiang, Lin; Zheng, Wenxin; Li, Ning; Hu, Wenping
abstract: CRISPR/Cas gene editing holds great promise for applications in agricultural breeding and gene therapy; however, native Cas proteins face bottlenecks such as off-target effects, PAM limitations, and delivery challenges. This review explores a three-tiered, progressive, and synergistic analytical framework comprising directed evolution, rational structural design, and integrated protein engineering. Following the logic of "random exploration-precision modification-system integration," it systematically clarifies the principles, advantages, disadvantages, and complementary interactions among these three optimization techniques. By comprehensively mapping the entire technical pathway for Cas protein improvement, this study fills a gap in systematic analysis within the field and provides a theoretical framework for tiered, synergistic modification to support the development of high-performance editors. The paper further analyzes a novel research and development paradigm in which AI and protein language models profoundly empower Cas modification. It summarizes intelligent toolchains such as structure prediction, virtual mutation, and de novo design of artificial Cas proteins, and highlights the unique advantages of AI in overcoming the performance trade-offs inherent in traditional protein engineering. At the same time, it identifies existing challenges, such as data scarcity and insufficient model interpretability, and looks ahead to how multimodal gene-editing large language models and automated closed-loop experimental systems will drive the iterative development of miniaturized, broad-spectrum, and highly precise editing tools, thereby facilitating the clinical and industrial implementation of gene-editing technologies.

title: Structural Empowerment Sensing: Decoding the Structure-Activity Relationship and Detection Application of G‑Quadruplex Aptamer.
authors: Bao, Wenji; Su, Ailing; Ao, Denggerile; Ga, Lu; Yu, Lan; Ai, Jun
abstract: G-Quadruplex (G4) aptamers have emerged as versatile functional nucleic acid architectures for biosensing because of their unique conformational plasticity, programmable topologies, and intrinsic signal-regulation capabilities. Unlike conventional recognition elements that mainly function as passive binding scaffolds, G4 aptamers can actively regulate signal generation and transduction through topology-dependent structural dynamics. Increasing evidence indicates that biosensing performance is closely governed by conformational energetics, folding kinetics, loop organization, ion coordination, and nano-interfacial coupling. This review summarizes recent advances in structure-guided G4 aptamer biosensing from the perspective of "structural empowerment", where conformational architectures directly determine sensing behavior and analytical output. We first discuss the structural fundamentals of G4 aptamers, including topology diversity, thermodynamic stability, folding pathways, and environmental responsiveness, emphasizing their influence on molecular recognition and signal accessibility. We then analyze the mechanistic relationship between G4 conformational transitions and multiple signal transduction modes, including fluorescence, electrochemical, colorimetric, surface-enhanced Raman scattering, photoelectrochemical, and catalytic sensing systems. Particular attention is given to the integration of G4 architectures with CRISPR platforms, nanozymes, DNA amplification circuits, metal-organic frameworks, and nanointerfacial engineering strategies. Importantly, this review establishes a structure-performance framework correlating G4 topological features and kinetic behaviors with analytical outcomes. Current limitations, including structural polymorphism, ionic dependence, reproducibility issues, and limited quantitative predictability, are critically discussed. Finally, future opportunities in adaptive biosensing, intelligent molecular interfaces, and AI-assisted structural design are highlighted. This review establishes a quantitative structure-performance framework by correlating G4 structural descriptors, conformational energetics, kinetic parameters, and analytical outputs, providing a basis for predictive design of G4-based sensing systems.

title: Nucleoredoxin proteins in green lineage: Insights about its roles in biotic and abiotic stress resilience.
authors: Gupta, Arvind; Thakur, Rahul; Yadav, Saurabh
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
abstract: Oxidative stress and reactive oxygen species (ROS) in plants are inevitable, and plants employ enzymatic and non-enzymatic system for cell homeostasis. Nucleoredoxins (NRX) are a family of thioredoxin (TRX) superfamily and being nuclear oxidoreductase, NRX are an important class of proteins present in many organisms including plants. Unlike TRXs, plant NRXs are larger proteins comprising of multiple TRX domains and conserved active redox motif 'WCPPC', displayed evolutionary conservation across various plants. NRX maintains oxidative stress tolerance by maintaining the reduced state by thiol-disulphide chemistry via conserved cysteine residues present in active site. Subcellular localization of NRX is mostly cytoplasmic and the putative protein interacting partners predicted their correlation with oxidative stress tolerance. We have also attempted to correlate plant NRXs with the available patent documents and observed that very little information is available. Compared to TRX research that started in 1960s, NRX have been discovered later and their structural complexity, multiple isoforms have led to their functional characterization more challenging. NRXs have roles in abiotic and biotic stresses and emerging roles indicate its role in plant immunity and modulation of plant defense response at molecular level by -OMICS studies. In view of the above, the present review discusses the sequence analysis, structure, and functional genomics associated with NRXs in plants. This is also correlated with the futuristic aspect of NRX roles being delineated in molecular stress response and signaling using CRISPR-Cas genome editing and related techniques.

title: Exonuclease-gated CRISPR/Cas12a biosensing strategy for sensitive detection of lncRNA MIR155HG.
authors: Wang, Qiufeng; Cai, Yongliang; Zhu, Shiyu; Yin, Feifan; Jiang, Yihao; Sun, Heliang; Xiang, Yang; Wang, Zhongyun
journal: Journal of pharmaceutical and biomedical analysis
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have been shown to be important regulatory factors in initiation and progression of cancer. However, sensitive detection of lncRNAs remains challenging due to their low abundance, complex structure and susceptibility to nuclease degradation. Among various lncRNAs, MIR155HG has been shown to be involved in the progression of cervical cancer and serve as a potential target for biomarker analysis. Here, we developed an exonuclease-gated CRISPR/Cas12a biosensing platform (E-CRISPR) for the detection of MIR155HG without target pre-amplification. This strategy relies on a bifunctional single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) probe containing both a MIR155HG recognition region and a CRISPR/Cas12a activation region. In the absence of target RNA, exonuclease I (Exo I) degrades the ssDNA probe, thereby reducing background signals. Upon binding to MIR155HG, RNA-DNA hybridization reduces the probe's susceptibility to Exo I digestion and allows the retained probe to activate CRISPR/Cas12a and generate an enhanced fluorescence signal. Under optimized conditions, the E-CRISPR assay achieved a limit of detection of 4.76 pM and a linear range of 4.76 pM to 0.4 nM. The entire assay could be completed within 100 min while maintaining sensitive detection of MIR155HG and showed good sequence specificity and reliable performance in complex biological environment. This exonuclease-regulated CRISPR/Cas12a strategy provides a simple analytical approach for extracellular lncRNA analysis.

title: CRISPR/Cas12a-Based Aptasensor for Cas9 Protein Detection in Spiked Food Matrices.
authors: Wang, Zizhao; Wang, Jing; Li, Ling; Chen, Guofeng; Wen, Hongtao; Liu, Baohai; Dong, Yiyang
abstract: Residual gene editors are a concern associated with the widespread application of CRISPR/Cas9 technology. Here, we developed a CRISPR/Cas12a-based fluorescent aptasensor for the qualitative and quantitative detection of Cas9 protein. Secondary structure prediction and molecular docking were combined to identify potential binding sites of the Cas9-specific aptamer. A fluorescence aptasensor was constructed based on competitive binding: in the presence of Cas9, the aptamer binds to the target and releases complementary DNA (cDNA), which activates the trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a. Cas12a subsequently cleaves a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) reporter labeled with a fluorophore and a quencher, generating a fluorescence signal, expressed in relative fluorescence units (RFU), that increases with Cas9 concentration. The optimized conditions comprised a trans-cleavage reaction time of 20 min, a Cas12a:CRISPR RNA (crRNA) molar ratio of 1:1, a final aptamer concentration of 180 nM, and a combination of low- and high-salt buffers to balance molecular recognition and protein stability. The proposed assay enabled Cas9 protein detection in buffer and Cas9-spiked soybean milk and cereal matrices. These results represent a proof-of-concept evaluation in complex food matrices rather than validation of authentic residual Cas9 detection. Further studies using unspiked gene-edited samples with independently verified Cas9 residues and an orthogonal reference method are required.

title: Type III Effectors of Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000: Molecular Mechanisms, Host Manipulation Networks, and Implications for Plant Disease Resistance.
abstract: Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000 (Pst DC3000) is a reference system for dissecting how type III-secreted effectors (T3Es) suppress plant immunity and reconfigure host physiology. Here, we reassess the DC3000 effector repertoire through an evidence-graded framework that links experimentally resolved effector-target mechanisms to repertoire-level genetic interactions and, ultimately, to disease-resistance strategies. We distinguish findings demonstrated with Pst DC3000 from mechanistic examples derived from other P. syringae pathovars and from computationally generated hypotheses. At the molecular level, validated DC3000 effectors perturb pattern-recognition receptor signaling, protein turnover, vesicle trafficking, plasmodesmatal communication, organelle function, and hormone-associated processes. At the repertoire level, deletion and reconstruction studies reveal functional redundancy, specialization, conditional suppression, and context-dependent interactions; importantly, convergence on a common host phenotype is not treated as evidence of direct physical cooperation between effectors. We further evaluate how effectoromics, multi-omics, single-cell and spatial approaches, structure prediction, and machine-learning tools can prioritize new hypotheses while emphasizing their need for genetic, biochemical, and infection-based validation. Finally, we consider how conserved effector targets, susceptibility factors, NLR engineering, and CRISPR-based editing may translate mechanistic knowledge into more durable bacterial-disease resistance. This synthesis positions the DC3000 system as a bridge between mechanistic effector biology, quantitative effector-network analysis, and experimentally testable strategies for crop protection.
